title: The True Vine, Friends of Jesus, and the Hatred of the World
summary: Jesus calls himself the true vine and his Father the vinedresser, and urges the disciples to remain in him, since branches cut off from the vine can bear no fruit. He commands them to love one another as he has loved them, and calls them no longer servants but friends. He warns them that the world will hate them as it hated him, and promises that the Advocate, the Spirit of truth, will testify about him, as they also must.
story: Chapter 14 ended with “Let us go on from here” (14:31), and chapter 15 continues the farewell teaching, whether still at the table or on the way out of the city toward the Mount of Olives. Where chapter 14 focused on Jesus' going and the comfort of his return, chapter 15 turns to life in the meantime: how the disciples are to live connected to him while he is absent, how they are to treat one another, and what they will face from the world. The chapter moves from intimacy (vine and branches, friends) to opposition (the world's hatred), and it ends with the Spirit and the disciples as joint witnesses. The two belong together; union with Jesus brings both his love and his rejection.
historical:
The vine was one of Israel's national symbols. Josephus, the first-century Jewish historian, describes a great golden vine with grape clusters as large as a man, set above the entrance to the sanctuary of Herod's temple, and grapevines appeared on Jewish coins of the later revolts against Rome. Jesus' disciples would have known the image both from Scripture and from the temple itself.

The warnings about hatred and persecution (15:18-25) look ahead to what the disciples will face. The book of Acts records the apostles' arrests and floggings by the temple authorities, the stoning of Stephen, the execution of James the son of Zebedee under Herod Agrippa I around AD 44, and Paul's many trials before both Jewish and Roman authorities. Later, Christians would be persecuted by Rome itself, notably under Nero in the mid-60s. The world here, as throughout John, is humanity organized against God, not a particular people. That matters because the phrase “their Law” (15:25) could be read as setting Jesus against Judaism; in fact it quotes Israel's own psalms as a witness on Jesus' behalf, and Jesus and all the disciples he addresses are Jews.
cultural:
Vineyards covered the hillsides of Judea and Galilee, and every listener knew how they worked. In late winter or early spring the vinedresser cut away dead or barren branches and pruned fruitful ones so that the plant's strength would go into grapes rather than leaves. The cut wood of a vine was useless for building or carving; it was fit only to be burned (Ezekiel 15:1-8 makes exactly this point). A branch had life only as long as it stayed joined to the vine.

Friendship in the ancient world had rich associations. The friends of a king were his trusted inner circle, who knew his plans, in contrast to slaves who simply carried out orders. Abraham was called the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8; 2 Chronicles 20:7), and Moses spoke with God as a man speaks with his friend (Exodus 33:11). Greek moral writers, such as Aristotle, discussed friendship at length and praised the friend who would die for another. Jesus draws on this language but grounds it in his own act: he lays down his life for his friends.
literary: The chapter opens with the last of John's seven “I am” sayings with an image: “I am the true vine” (15:1), repeated in 15:5. The key word is remain (menō), used eleven times in 15:1-17, which binds the section together. The vine image is not a parable with a story but an extended metaphor that Jesus explains as he goes. The second half (15:18-27) turns from love to hate: the verb hate appears seven times. The two halves mirror each other, since the love that joins the disciples to Jesus and to one another is what sets them apart from the world. The quotation “They hated Me without reason” (15:25) comes from the Psalms (35:19; 69:4), which John calls their Law, using the word in its broad sense for Israel's Scriptures.

outline.t: The vine and the branches: remain in me
Remain in my love: friends of Jesus
The Spirit and the disciples will testify

doctrines.note: The Advocate is “the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father” and whom Jesus will send from the Father (15:26). This verse was central to the long dispute between Eastern and Western churches over the filioque, the Western addition to the Nicene Creed saying the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The East holds that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone; the West sees the Son's sending of the Spirit as reflecting an eternal relation. Both confess the Spirit as fully God.
The branches are joined to the vine and so to one another. The church's life depends on union with Christ, “for apart from Me you can do nothing” (15:5), and its mark is love modeled on his.

“If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first” (15:18). Jesus prepares his followers for opposition as the normal consequence of belonging to him. Suffering for his name is not a sign that something has gone wrong.

words.note: Menō, to remain, abide, or stay. It is one of John's favorite words, used eleven times in this chapter. It describes a settled, continuing relationship: the branch remaining in the vine, the disciples remaining in Jesus' love, his words remaining in them. It is less about a feeling than about staying connected.

Karpos, fruit. In the Bible fruit often stands for the visible results of a life, good or bad (Matthew 7:16-20; Galatians 5:22-23). Here it likely includes both character, especially love and obedience, and the fruit of mission, people brought to faith. The fruit is the Father's glory (15:8).

Philos, friend, related to phileō, to love. Jesus calls the disciples friends because he has made known to them everything he learned from the Father (15:15). Friendship with Jesus does not erase his authority, since they are friends if they do what he commands, but it transforms obedience from servitude into shared purpose.

Miseō, to hate. It appears seven times in 15:18-25. In John the world's hatred of Jesus and his followers is the dark counterpart of the Father's love. The Bible sometimes uses hate in a comparative sense (to love less), but here it means active hostility.

christ: In the Old Testament Israel was God's vine, planted with care but often producing bad fruit (Psalm 80:8-16; Isaiah 5:1-7; Jeremiah 2:21). When Jesus says “I am the true vine,” he claims to be what Israel was meant to be, the faithful people of God in one person, bearing the fruit God looked for. Those joined to him become part of God's vineyard. He is also the friend who shows the greatest love: “Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends” (15:13), spoken hours before he did exactly that.

hard.q: Branches that do not remain are thrown into the fire. Can a true believer be cut off and lost?
hard.a:
The chapter's warning (15:2, 6) is taken seriously in every Christian tradition, but it is read differently. Many in the Reformed and Baptist traditions hold that those truly united to Christ will be kept by God to the end (compare 10:28-29), and they read the fruitless branches as people who had outward association with Jesus but never true union, as Judas did. Wesleyan, Arminian, and many Catholic and Orthodox readers take the warning as a real possibility: believers can, by persistent unbelief, cease to remain in Christ and be lost. Some interpreters also note that the verb in 15:2 (airō) can mean to lift up as well as to cut off, and suggest a vinedresser lifting a trailing branch off the ground, though most scholars think cutting off fits the context better.

Every reading agrees on the chapter's main point: life comes only from remaining in Christ, and the warning is meant to drive disciples to stay close to him, not to make them anxious about their standing. The question of whether a true believer can finally fall away is a second-order one on which faithful churches differ.

questions: Jesus says, “apart from Me you can do nothing.” Where are you trying to bear fruit in your own strength?
Pruning cuts away even healthy growth so that the plant bears more fruit. What might God be pruning in your life, and how do you respond to it?
Jesus calls his disciples friends. How would your prayers and obedience change if you took that seriously?
